To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have determined the high resolution structures of the quorum sensing receptor LasR bound to the autoinducer 3-oxo-C12-HSL, and to the small molecule quorum-sensing modulators TP-1,TP-3, andTP-4.

the triphenyl compounds TP-1 and TP-4 interact with the LasR receptor by binding in the autoinducer binding pocket, with TP-1 binding to the receptor in a manner that is similar to that observed for N-3- oxo-dodecanoly homoserine lacton, and with TP-4 binding to the receptor with a different conformation that is stabilized by the formation of a new hydrogen bond.

the LasR receptor binds structurally distinct compounds with similar affinities, and that the LasR ligand binding domain accommodates the triphenyl compounds by a combination of induced-fit and conformational change.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new small molecule inhibitors of bacterial virulence factors.
the identification and development of novel quinolones as antibacterials and anti-virulence agents.

understanding and exploiting the mechanisms of bacterial communication and virulence regulation, and has led to the discovery of novel small molecules that can be used to modulate quorumsensing in Pseudomonas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the triphenyl compounds are mimics of the homoserine autoinducer, and are able to bind LasR with a high affinity, but that the tripheny compounds bind in a different orientation than the homoserine, and that the binding mode of the triphenyls is different from the autoinducer, as evidenced by the differences in the binding modes and the lack of a conserved hydrogen bond network.

the crystal structures of the LasR ligand binding domains in complex with the structurally distinct ligands N-3- oxo-dodecanolyl homoserine lactones, and the triphenyl autoinducer mimetics, provide molecular insights into the structural determinants for ligand binding, and provide the basis for the development of small-molecule quorum-sensing modulators.

these structures reveal the molecular basis for the recognition by LasR of structurally distinct small-molecule autoinhibitor mimics, and provide the structural framework for the design and development of novel quorm sensing regulators.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified and characterized a novel class of small-molecule quorum-sensing antagonists.

we are developing novel small-molecules that can be used to modulate quorom sensing, which is a process that is used by bacteria to coordinate their virulence factors, and that we are doing this through the use of structural biology.

we have identified a class compounds that can be used to regulate virulence in P. aeruginosa and that we have determined the molecular basis of their interaction with the LasR quorum sensing receptor.
The main takeaway from our work is that

LasR is capable of accommodating a wide range of structurally diverse molecules in its ligand binding site, including the autoinducer and the structurally distinct triphenyl compounds, and that the structural basis for this promiscuity is a combination of plasticity of the receptor and flexibility of the ligand.
the LasR receptor can accommodate structurally diverse molecules, including those with no chemical similarities to the natural autoinducer, by adopting multiple conformational states.
the LasR receptor is able to bind a wide variety of structurally distinct compounds with high specificity.
